question_html: What is a Single Entry System of bookkeeping fundamentally considered to be?

options.A: A standardized scientific double-entry accounting method
options.B: A system of incomplete or improper records
options.C: A mandatory statutory requirement for corporate entities

answer_html: Answer: (B) There is no such formal system as Single-Entry System as the accounts can only be prepared using Double Entry System; it is truly a system of incomplete or improper records[cite: 19].

question_html: Which of the following is an alternative name for the method of determining profit by capital comparison?

options.A: Net Worth Method or Statement of Affairs Method

answer_html: Answer: (A) Ascertainment of profit by capital comparison is also known as the Net Worth method or Statement of Affairs Method[cite: 19].
topic_text: Ascertainment of Profit by Capital Comparison

question_html: In a pure single entry system, what accounts are maintained?

options.C: Personal accounts, cash book, and subsidiary books
options.D: All real, nominal, and personal accounts

answer_html: Answer: (A) In pure single entry, only personal accounts are maintained with no information regarding cash and bank balances[cite: 19].

question_html: Which type of single-entry system maintains personal accounts, a cash book, and some subsidiary books like sales and purchases books?
answer_html: Answer: (C) In quasi single entry, personal accounts, cash book, and some subsidiary books (such as sales book and purchases book) are maintained[cite: 19].

question_html: What does a Statement of Affairs prepared under incomplete records represent?

options.B: A statement of assets and liabilities used to find capital
options.C: A certified profit and loss statement

answer_html: Answer: (B) A Statement of Affairs lists assets and liabilities to determine capital balances (where capital is the balancing figure)[cite: 19].

question_html: How is capital computed using assets and liabilities?

options.D: Capital = Current Assets minus Current Liabilities only

answer_html: Answer: (B) Capital is calculated as Assets minus outside liabilities[cite: 19].

question_html: When computing profit under the Net Worth method, how are drawings treated with respect to closing capital?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Drawings reduce capital during the year, so they are added back when computing profit from closing capital[cite: 19].

question_html: How is fresh capital introduced treated when calculating profit under the net worth method?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing capital increases if fresh capital is introduced, so it is deducted to find operational profit[cite: 19].

question_html: Which of the following is a key difference between a Statement of Affairs and a Balance Sheet?

options.A: A Balance Sheet is based on strict double-entry records, whereas a Statement of Affairs is based partly on incomplete records and estimates.
options.B: A Statement of Affairs always tallies automatically without balancing figures.
options.C: A Balance Sheet can have omitted items easily, whereas a Statement of Affairs cannot.
options.D: There is no difference between them.

answer_html: Answer: (A) A Balance Sheet is based on transactions strictly recorded under double entry, whereas a Statement of Affairs is prepared from partly recorded data and estimates[cite: 19].
topic_text: Statement of Affairs vs Balance Sheet

question_html: In a Total Debtors Account, what does the balancing figure usually represent if credit sales are missing?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Credit sales can be ascertained as the balancing figure in the Total Debtors Account if all other ledger components are known[cite: 19].

question_html: In a Total Creditors Account, what does the balancing figure typically represent when purchases are missing?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Credit purchases are found as the balancing figure in the Total Creditors Account[cite: 19].

question_html: How should household or personal expenses paid out of business cash be treated?

options.B: Treated as drawings and debited to the proprietor's capital account
options.D: Credited to cash account as miscellaneous income

answer_html: Answer: (B) Household expenses paid from business cash are treated as drawings and debited to capital[cite: 19].

question_html: If a proprietor brings in money collected on the maturity of their personal Life Insurance Policy into the business, how should it be accounted for?

options.B: As fresh capital introduced by the proprietor

answer_html: Answer: (B) Money put into the business from maturity of private policies represents fresh capital invested by the proprietor[cite: 19].

question_html: Why can't a Trial Balance be reliably drawn up directly from books kept under a pure single entry system?

options.A: Because real and nominal accounts are generally omitted, violating double-entry duality.
options.B: Because banks do not allow trial balances.
options.C: Because computers cannot process single entry numbers.
options.D: Because trial balances are only for corporations.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Since real and nominal accounts are largely omitted and duality is ignored, a standard trial balance cannot be directly drawn up[cite: 19].

question_html: What is the recommended approach when an accountant is asked to prepare final accounts from incomplete records?

options.A: Convert the records to double entry by reconstructing accounts and preparing a trial balance
options.B: Guess the profit figure based on industry averages
options.C: Only prepare a receipts and payments summary and stop

answer_html: Answer: (A) It is advisable to first convert records to the double entry system, complete posting, draw up a trial balance, and then prepare final accounts[cite: 19].
topic_text: Techniques of Obtaining Complete Accounting Information

question_html: Raju has opening capital of ₹10,000, closing capital of ₹12,500, drawings during the year of ₹3,000, and additional capital added of ₹3,750. What is the net profit or loss for the year?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Closing capital ($12,500) + Drawings ($3,000) - Additional capital ($3,750) - Opening capital ($10,000) = ₹1,750 net profit[cite: 19].

question_html: Rakesh started business on April 1, 2021 with capital of ₹1,00,000. On March 31, 2022, his assets/liabilities were: Cash ₹3,200, Inventory ₹34,800, Debtors ₹31,000, Machine ₹85,000, Creditors ₹12,000, Bank loan ₹10,000. Drawings made during the year were ₹24,000. What is the profit for the year?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing capital = (3,200 + 34,800 + 31,000 + 85,000) - (12,000 + 10,000) = ₹1,32,000. Profit = Closing capital ($1,32,000) + Drawings ($24,000) - Opening capital ($1,00,000) = ₹56,000[cite: 19].
topic_text: Statement of Affairs and Profit Determination

question_html: Calculate bad debts from the following: Opening debtors ₹5,00,000, Closing debtors ₹7,00,000, Cash received ₹6,00,000, Discount allowed ₹10,000, Credit sales ₹11,40,000, Bills receivable drawn ₹3,00,000.
answer_html: Answer: (C) Total debits in Debtors A/c = 5,00,000 + 11,40,000 = 16,40,000. Total known credits (Cash + Discount + BR + Closing balance) = 6,00,000 + 10,000 + 3,00,000 + 7,00,000 = 16,10,000. Balancing figure for Bad Debts = 16,40,000 - 16,10,000 = ₹30,000[cite: 19].

question_html: Calculate credit purchases from the following: Opening creditors ₹4,00,000, Closing creditors ₹5,00,000, Cash paid to creditors ₹8,50,000, Discount received ₹20,000.
answer_html: Answer: (A) Creditors A/c total debits (Cash + Discount + Closing balance) = 8,50,000 + 20,000 + 5,00,000 = 13,70,000. Less opening balance (4,00,000) = Credit Purchases of ₹9,70,000[cite: 19].

question_html: A firm sold 20% of goods on cash basis and the balance on credit. Debtors are allowed 1.5 months credit and their balance as on 31.03.2021 was ₹1,25,000 (assume uniform monthly sales). What are the total sales of the company for the year ended 31.03.2022?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Credit Sales = Debtors $\times (12 / 1.5) = 1,25,000 \times 8 = 10,000,000$ (Wait, $1,25,000 \times 12 / 1.5 = 10,00,000$). Since credit sales are 80% of total sales, Total Sales = $10,000,000 / 0.8 = \text{₹}12,50,000$[cite: 19].

question_html: Ram sells goods at a profit of 25% on sales. Opening stock is ₹2,80,000, cash sales ₹2,40,000, credit sales ₹10,00,000, cash purchases ₹20,000, payments to creditors ₹7,00,000. What is the total sales?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Total Sales = Cash Sales ($2,40,000$) + Credit Sales ($10,000,000$) = ₹12,40,000[cite: 19].

question_html: In an incomplete records problem, opening capital is calculated as ₹26,770, net profit is ₹4,290, additional capital paid into bank is ₹8,500, and household expenses drawn are ₹3,180. What is the closing capital?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Closing capital = Opening capital ($26,770$) + Additional capital ($8,500$) + Net Profit ($4,290$) - Drawings ($3,180$) = ₹36,380[cite: 19].

question_html: Mr. Anup's business reports opening inventory of ₹1,10,000, closing inventory of ₹1,90,000, net credit purchases of ₹4,49,900, and net credit sales of ₹9,58,550. What is the gross profit?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Trading account gross profit balancing figure is ₹5,88,650[cite: 19].

question_html: Lucky sells goods at cost plus 25%. Cost of goods sold was ₹2,60,000. What is the sales amount?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Sales = Cost ($2,60,000) \times (125 / 100) = ₹3,25,000[cite: 19].

question_html: Mr. A's sales for the year ended 31st March, 2022 were 20% higher than previous year's sales of ₹5,00,000. If 20% of total sales were cash sales, what is the amount of credit sales?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Total sales for 2021-22 = 5,00,000 + 20% = ₹6,00,000. Credit sales = 80% of total sales = $6,00,000 \times 0.8 = \text{₹}4,80,000$[cite: 19].

question_html: Why do small sole proprietorships often maintain incomplete records?

options.A: Lack of knowledge of formal double-entry accounting or to save time and effort
options.B: Mandatory orders from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal
options.C: Strict statutory enforcement of single-entry laws
options.D: To eliminate the need for bank accounts

answer_html: Answer: (A) Small businesses may not maintain double entry due to lack of accounting knowledge or unwillingness to spend time/effort[cite: 19].

question_html: What source documents or records does an accountant typically use to find cash and bank balances when reconstructing accounts?

options.A: Cash book and bank pass book

answer_html: Answer: (A) Cash book for cash balance and bank pass book for bank balance are primary sources utilized[cite: 19].

question_html: Are profits computed under a single-entry system considered precise and exact?

options.B: No, they are only estimates based on available information, so true profits cannot be determined with certainty.
options.C: Yes, because tax authorities audit them strictly.
options.D: They are always higher than double-entry profits.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Profit under this system is only an estimate based on available information and therefore true and correct profits cannot be determined directly[cite: 19].

question_html: How is closing stock usually verified for incomplete records when physical inventory is lacking?

options.B: By guessing a flat 10% of sales

answer_html: Answer: (A) Inventory is determined by actual counting and valuation[cite: 19].

question_html: What should be done with discounts allowed when analyzing a sales ledger in single entry reconstruction?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Discounts allowed reduce the debtor balance and are credited to the Total Debtors Account[cite: 19].

question_html: How are bills receivable dishonored treated in a Total Debtors Account?
answer_html: Answer: (A) When bills are dishonored, the debtor's balance is reinstated by debiting the Total Debtors Account[cite: 19].

question_html: What is the effect of bad debts written off on the Total Debtors Account?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Bad debts written off reduce trade debtors and are credited to the Total Debtors Account[cite: 19].

question_html: Why are purchase ledgers not as commonly maintained as debtor ledgers in simple single entry systems?

options.A: Because it is often convenient to record liabilities when paid rather than when incurred.
options.B: Because creditors do not give credit.
options.D: Because suppliers do not send bills.

answer_html: Answer: (A) A Purchases Ledger is not as commonly maintained because it is convenient to make entries for liabilities when paid[cite: 19].

question_html: How should rent of premises used jointly for business and proprietor's residence be treated?

options.A: Allocated equitably between business expense and proprietor's drawings based on area/usage

answer_html: Answer: (A) When the benefit is received by both, rent should be allocated on some equitable basis like area occupied[cite: 19].

question_html: What does a cash book that mixes up personal transactions of the owner with business transactions indicate?

options.A: A feature of unscientific single-entry recording

answer_html: Answer: (A) Mixing business and personal transactions in the cash book is a characteristic feature of single entry systems[cite: 19].

question_html: Mr. B's closing capital on 31.3.2022 was ₹4,00,000. On 1.4.2021, his capital was ₹3,50,000. Net profit for the year was ₹1,00,000. He introduced ₹30,000 as additional capital in February 2022. What was the amount drawn by Mr. B for domestic expenses?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing Capital ($4,00,000$) = Opening ($3,50,000$) + Addl Capital ($30,000$) + Profit ($1,00,000$) - Drawings. $4,00,000 = 4,80,000 - \text{Drawings}$, hence Drawings = ₹80,000[cite: 19].

question_html: Given: Opening capital ₹60,000, Drawings ₹5,000, Capital introduced ₹10,000, Closing capital ₹90,000. What is the profit earned during the period?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Profit = Closing Capital ($90,000$) + Drawings ($5,000$) - Additional Capital ($10,000$) - Opening Capital ($60,000$) = ₹25,000[cite: 19].

question_html: In A. Adamjee's business, opening stock is ₹3,900, purchases are ₹49,100, and sales total ₹62,100 (including ₹11,000 cash sales and credit sales of ₹51,100). If closing inventory is ₹5,700, what is the gross profit?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Trading account gross profit = Credit Side ($62,100 + 5,700$) - Debit Side ($3,900 + 49,100$) = ₹14,800[cite: 19].

question_html: In A. Adamjee's business, machinery is valued at ₹7,500 and furniture at ₹1,200. If depreciation is provided at 10% per annum on both, what is the total depreciation expense?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Machinery depreciation = $750$. Furniture depreciation = $120$. Total = ₹870[cite: 19].

question_html: Mr. Manoj paid cash expenses of ₹9,570 during the year. Outstanding expenses at the end were ₹330 and at the beginning were ₹600. What amount should be charged to the Profit and Loss Account for sundry expenses?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Cash paid ($9,570$) + Closing outstanding ($330$) - Opening outstanding ($600$) = ₹9,300[cite: 19].

question_html: Lucky sold fixed assets of book value ₹2,500 for ₹1,750. What is the loss on sale of fixed assets?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Book value ($2,500$) - Sale proceeds ($1,750$) = ₹750 loss[cite: 19].
topic_text: Loss on Sale of Fixed Assets

question_html: Ram took a loan of ₹1,00,000 on 1.10.2021 at 10% per annum (accounting year ends 31.3.2022). What is the total loan liability including interest due on 31.3.2022?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Principal ($1,00,000$) + Interest for 6 months ($1,00,000 \times 10\% \times 6/12 = 5,000$) = ₹1,05,000[cite: 19].

question_html: In Mr. A's reconstruction, bank payments to creditors were ₹3,00,000, rent paid up to March 31, 2022 was ₹16,000, cash deposited into bank was ₹80,000. If opening bank balance was ₹38,000 and total debits to bank were ₹5,78,000, what is the closing bank balance?
answer_html: Answer: (A) Bank Account closing balance balancing figure is ₹2,62,000[cite: 19].

question_html: In Shri Moti's assessment case, if capital on 1.4.2020 was ₹3,13,000, domestic expenditure for two years was ₹96,000, capital on 1.4.2022 was ₹5,65,000, what is the total true income earned over the two years?
answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing Capital ($5,65,000$) + Drawings ($96,000$) - Opening Capital ($3,13,000$) = ₹3,48,000[cite: 19].

question_html: Can limited liability companies legally maintain their books entirely under a single-entry system?

options.B: No, legal requirements mandate companies to maintain proper double-entry accounting records.
options.C: Only during the first year of incorporation.
options.D: Yes, if turnover is below a threshold.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Single entry system is never used for limited liability companies on account of legal requirements[cite: 19].

question_html: What is the valuation basis of fixed assets in a Statement of Affairs compared to a proper Balance Sheet?

options.A: In a Statement of Affairs, asset valuation is often arbitrary or estimated, whereas in a Balance Sheet, fixed assets are shown at original cost less depreciation on a scientific basis.
options.B: Both use identical certified market values.
options.C: Statement of Affairs uses replacement cost exclusively.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Valuation in a statement of affairs is often arbitrary, whereas a balance sheet shows fixed assets at original cost less depreciation scientifically[cite: 19].

question_html: What does the term 'Quasi Single Entry' imply regarding subsidiary books?

options.A: Personal accounts, cash book, and some subsidiary books like sales and purchases books are maintained.
options.B: No books of original entry are ever kept.

answer_html: Answer: (A) Quasi single entry involves maintaining personal accounts, cash book, and subsidiary books like sales and purchases books[cite: 19].

question_html: How are discount columns in a cash book treated when completing double entry from incomplete records?

options.A: Totals of discounts paid and received should be posted to Discounts Allowed and Discounts Received Accounts.

answer_html: Answer: (A) If there are discount columns, totals of discounts paid and received must be posted to respective discount accounts to complete double entry[cite: 19].

question_html: What is the objective of preparing a Balance Sheet under double-entry compared to a Statement of Affairs?

options.A: A Balance Sheet ascertains the true financial position on a date, whereas a Statement of Affairs primarily aims to identify capital figures at the beginning/end.
options.B: A Statement of Affairs is used for tax evasion.
options.C: A Balance Sheet is only an estimate.
options.D: There is no difference in objectives.

answer_html: Answer: (A) The objective of a balance sheet is to ascertain financial position, while a statement of affairs primarily identifies capital figures[cite: 19].

question_html: How should unidentified cash shortages or withdrawals made without entry be treated in single-entry reconstructions?

options.A: Debited to the proprietor's capital account as drawings

answer_html: Answer: (A) If cash is short because the proprietor withdrew money without entry, the proprietor's capital account should be debited[cite: 19].
